segments.text: Let's say your season-end basketball tournament starts next week, and you need to review the league rules to prepare.
Instead of reading the massive 200-page league rulebook yourself, you upload the PDF to an AI for a quick summary.
You type in a straightforward question. How many fouls until I'm out of the game?
The AI replies with confidence. Five fouls and you foul out.
But wait a second. You remember last year's tournament where a player picked up five fouls and was allowed to stay on the court.
So you open the document and dig through the physical pages yourself to find out what happened.
You find the regular season rule. Five fouls. Exactly what the AI stated.
But near the end of the book, there's a special section specifically for tournaments. In those games players get six fouls.
The AI didn't hallucinate or invent a fake rule. It provided a factually correct answer that was entirely incomplete.
This is the document trap. The dangerous assumption that uploading a file is the exact same thing as the AI fully reading it.
To understand why this happens, we have to look at the AI's context window.
This is the system's active workspace, and it strictly limits how much text it can analyze it any one time.
A short, one-page file might fade into that workspace in full. But a massive 200-page rulebook simply will not.
When you ask a question about a long document, the AI doesn't read the whole thing.
It switches to a search and filter retrieval process, scanning to locate isolated passages that match the exact freezing of your prompt,
pulling those specific sections into its workspace to generate an answer.
If we visualize this, the retrieval machine scans the basketball rulebook and selects a few specific pages containing the words fouls and out of the game.
But look at the pages left entirely behind.
The page containing the critical six-fowel tournament exception is bypassed completely.
Because the AI only formulates its answer based on the isolated pages it retrieved, it never even saw the exception.
Uploading a document does not guarantee the machine will process all of it.
If we look back at our original prompt, we can see exactly why the retrieval failed.
We asked a generic question about fouls and completely omitted the word tournament, which is the specific context we actually cared about.
To force the right context, we revise the prompt.
In tournament games, how many fouls are allowed? Quote the rule and any exceptions.
With the search target clearly defined, the AI successfully retrieves the tournament section and identifies the six-fowel limit.
We avoid errors using this framework.
First, name the section. Use the document's exact headings.
Second, ask one thing. Give a single clear question.
Third, share what matters. Paste only the relevant section.
Finally, ask for the quote. Demand verbatim text to verify against the original.
These four steps improve accuracy and help verify rules. But remember, they are navigation aids.
They help you steer the AI, but they do not eliminate its inherent retrieval limits.
Missing a foul limit in a recreational basketball league is a low stakes error.
The danger scales up dramatically when we apply this to real-world paperwork.
Apartment leases and employment contracts are highly vulnerable to the document trap.
The same is true for complex financial paperwork, like insurance policies and financial aid letters,
where AI retrieval errors happen frequently.
These legal and professional documents are built entirely around hidden conditions,
clauses, and exceptions that dictate how the baseline rules are applied.
Which brings us to the core rule, displayed right here. Uploaded doesn't mean fully read.
You have to explicitly ask for the rule and any exceptions to ensure you get the whole truth.
